newsitem.title: USA: Departing space factory gives shuttle crew a scare.
newsitem.headline: Departing space factory gives shuttle crew a scare.

text.p: A prototype space factory, released from shuttle Columbia, gave astronauts a scare on Friday as it passed close by the shuttle's cockpit.

The two-ton Wake Shield Facility came a little close for comfort as a gas powered thruster propelled it away from the shuttle. The astronauts watched in radio silence as the saucer-shaped satellite sailed by.

"Now that my heart is a little bit out of my throat I can tell you a little bit about the separation," shuttle skipper Ken Cockrell said, as the bright disc of the satellite receded in television views from the shuttle.
"We kept it in sight... at all times so we were assured of safe clearance, but I have to say the clearance was somewhere 10 feet or less going over the front windows and the left part of the nose."
The Wake Shield was released from the mechanical clutches of Columbia's 50-foot- (15 metre) long robot arm at 8:38 p.m. EST (2038 GMT).

The Wake Shield is designed to manufacture ultra-pure semiconductors for use in high-speed computer chips. The stainless steel, saucer-shaped spacecraft could eventually lead to the first commercial space factories, its designers said.

As the Wake Shield travels through the tenuous atmosphere 218 miles (350 km) up, the 12-foot (3.6 metre) diameter disc will create a vacuum behind the craft nearly 100 times better than that possible on earth.
The near-perfect vacuum will provide ideal conditions for the atom-by-atom manufacture of semiconductors, free of the contamination found in ground-based laboratories.
"It may make materials that are needed for high performance computers, for wireless radio communications or cellular phones," Jones said.

"All of these kinds of high performance chips that we need for our electronic information-age society might be able to be made more cheaply in space. The Wake Shield is a way to test that hypothesis."
The Wake Shield will fly about 35 miles (56 km) behind Columbia for three days before the shuttle crew return on Monday night to pick it up.

The University of Houston Space Vacuum Epitaxy Center and Space Industries Inc., which designed the Wake Shield, have made about $5 million in improvements to solve the technical problems that plagued its first two test flights.
On the Wake Shield's maiden flight in February 1994, problems with the attitude control system prevented its deployment and it remained on the end of the shuttle's robot arm.
The spacecraft was released into orbit on its second mission, in September 1995, but it suffered further attitude problems, and it's electronics overheated.
Despite the problems, the Wake Shield manufactured four of the seven planned semiconductor wafers. Project officials said the quality was far superior to ground-manufactured wafers.
Friday night's deployment was delayed about 30 minutes while controllers solved a few lingering technical problems.

This outing of the Wake Shield will be a make-or-break venture for the troubled project. NASA recently cancelled a fourth test flight of the satellite to make way for another shuttle visit to Russia's Mir space station.
"We believe this is going to be a very successful flight this time around," Alex Ignatiev, director of the Space Vacuum Epitaxy Center, said.

The Wake Shield is the second recoverable satellite deployed on this mission. A U.S.-German telescope was released from Columbia on Tuesday night and was continuing on Friday to make observations of the mysterious interstellar matter which lies between the stars.
